paragraphs: This study asks how file-based project memory and hybrid lexical retrieval compare in answer accuracy and total model cost when both operate under an identical full-section character budget. Two concrete implementations are audited: a ProjectMemoryRail that writes facts to an isolated markdown file and truncates by prefix, and an EnhancedMemoryRail that stores completed exchanges in process-local working memory and selects them via a weighted combination of Jaccard lexical similarity, temporal decay, access frequency, and importance. Both arms receive the same twenty adapted LongMemEval-S single-session questions, the same fact episodes, and the same qwen-plus model. At the restricted budget the baseline achieves zero correct answers while the enhanced rail reaches [[metric:public_small.enhanced.accuracy]], a gap of [[metric:public_small.accuracy_gain_pp]] percentage points. At the expanded budget the gap narrows to [[metric:public_large.accuracy_gain_pp]] percentage points but does not close. The accuracy gain is purchased through [[metric:public_small.enhanced.seed_model_calls]] model-backed memory-write calls per budget, inflating total tokens per question to [[metric:public_small.enhanced.tokens_per_question]] and [[metric:public_large.enhanced.tokens_per_question]] versus [[metric:public_small.baseline.tokens_per_question]] and [[metric:public_large.baseline.tokens_per_question]] for the baseline. Findings derive from a single run per budget; descriptive Wilson intervals quantify question-sampling uncertainty only. The dataset is an adapted slice, not the official LongMemEval benchmark.

Practitioners integrating large language models into long-running agent workflows face a recurring design choice: store accumulated project knowledge in a flat file that is cheap to write but brittle under context-window truncation, or invest model calls at write time to build a structured working memory from which relevant items can later be selected. The first approach minimises construction cost but exposes the system to deterministic information loss whenever the file exceeds the prompt budget. The second approach pays a substantial token cost up front but can surface the most relevant facts regardless of their original position. Despite the prevalence of both patterns in production tooling, controlled empirical comparisons that account for the full cost of memory construction remain scarce.

This paper presents an auditable systems study of that trade-off. The research question is: how do file-based project memory and hybrid retrieval compare in answer accuracy and total model cost under equal context-character budgets? Three sub-questions structure the investigation. RQ1 asks whether accuracy differs between the two arms when both receive the same character budget. RQ2 asks whether complete evidence recall is associated with correct answers, and whether partial evidence can suffice. RQ3 asks how total token cost, including memory-write calls, compares between the arms.

The study audits an existing implementation rather than proposing a new retrieval algorithm. Both arms receive identical facts, questions, model identity, and system prompt; only the memory-construction and selection protocol differ. The baseline writes facts to an isolated JIUWENSWARM.md file and presents a prefix-truncated view. The enhanced arm writes completed user-assistant exchanges to process-local L1 memory through model-backed conversations and selects items using a fixed lexical ranking. Neither arm employs learned embeddings, reflection modules, or external tools.

Three contributions follow from this design. First, we provide a paired, single-run empirical comparison on twenty adapted LongMemEval-S single-session questions at two character budgets, with full cost accounting that includes memory-write tokens. Second, we document that the accuracy gap narrows as the budget grows yet does not vanish, and we trace the residual gap to whole-item packing versus prefix truncation. Third, we catalogue the confounds—prefix order, file-metadata overhead, format differences, single-run design, and string-match scoring—that prevent over-generalisation of the observed gaps.

The scope is deliberately narrow. The experiments do not validate an end-to-end paper-generation pipeline, do not test multi-session reasoning or temporal updates, and do not compare against published memory systems. The adapted LongMemEval slice covers only single-session factual extraction. All reported intervals are descriptive Wilson intervals over the twenty selected questions; no significance test is claimed or justified by the single-run protocol.

Memory control and organisation for language-model agents has attracted several architectural proposals. MemGPT introduces an operating-system-inspired virtual context manager that moves information across memory tiers, demonstrating document analysis and multi-session chat scenarios [[cite:ref_959d6858d034c6e1]]. The present study's fixed L1 Rail does not implement MemGPT's autonomous virtual-memory controller; MemGPT serves only as conceptual context for the tiered-storage vocabulary. A-MEM creates structured notes and dynamically links and evolves memories following a Zettelkasten-inspired organisation [[cite:ref_1aacba116cbe3c5b]]. Our fixed lexical ranking lacks autonomous linking and evolution, and no empirical comparison to A-MEM was run. Generative Agents synthesise natural-language experience records into reflections and dynamically retrieve them for planning behaviour in an interactive simulation [[cite:ref_6e953134a3c04402]]. This study neither implements reflection or planning nor tests social behaviour; it draws only on the general notion of retrieving stored records at query time.

Evidence access and position effects constitute a second theme. Lost in the Middle demonstrates that relevant information position affects multi-document question answering and key-value retrieval in long contexts, with middle positions often harder to exploit [[cite:ref_9dbf664b6954efbc]]. That finding motivates attention to how information is placed within a prompt, but it does not establish that the prefix truncation observed in our baseline is caused by the same attentional phenomenon; the baseline failure is deterministic removal of text beyond the budget, not degraded attention to retained text. MemoryBank supports retrieval and updates for sustained personalised interaction, modelling forgetting and reinforcement influenced by elapsed time and importance [[cite:ref_713e886950406893]]. Our temporal-decay term is a simpler heuristic and does not replicate MemoryBank's companion evaluation or its reinforcement dynamics.

Evaluation of long-term interactive memory forms the third cluster. LongMemEval benchmarks chat assistants on extraction, multi-session reasoning, temporal reasoning, knowledge updates, and abstention, explicitly separating indexing, retrieval, and reading stages [[cite:ref_ab2c226739f2f52a]]. The submitted adaptation covers only a narrow single-session-user extraction slice converted into fixed fact episodes; it does not exercise multi-session reasoning, temporal reasoning, updates, or abstention, and the resulting scores are not official LongMemEval benchmark results. Together, these six sources frame the design space within which the present two-arm comparison sits, while none is replicated or empirically benchmarked here.

The experimental design contrasts two memory-construction and selection protocols while holding the fact content, question set, model, and system prompt constant. The operational difference is that the baseline commits facts to a flat file and presents them by deterministic prefix, whereas the enhanced arm commits facts through model-backed conversations into a capacity-limited working store and selects items by a weighted lexical score. Because the construction protocols differ—disk write versus [[metric:public_small.enhanced.seed_model_calls]] model calls per budget—the comparison isolates the joint effect of construction and selection, not selection alone. The renderer inserts a methodology diagram summarising the two arms; the prose below refers to it descriptively.

The baseline is the actual ProjectMemoryRail implementation. During the seeding phase, facts are written to an isolated JIUWENSWARM.md file on disk. At query time the runner reads that file, prepends file metadata (filename, modification timestamp, section header), and truncates the resulting string by prefix to the full-section character budget. No embedding retrieval, re-ranking, or learned selection is applied; the model sees exactly the first characters of the serialised file up to the limit. Both arms receive the same facts, questions, model (qwen-plus), system prompt, and no external tools. This design means that at a small budget the file metadata consumes a non-trivial fraction of the available characters, and any fact whose serialised position falls beyond the truncation boundary is deterministically absent from the prompt. The baseline is therefore not a retrieval-augmented embedding baseline; it is a prefix-truncated flat-file baseline whose failure mode is entirely order-dependent. Subsequent sections reference this truncation mechanism without restating it.

The enhanced arm is the EnhancedMemoryRail. During seeding, completed user-assistant exchanges are written to process-local L1 memory through model-backed conversations; the store has a capacity of twenty entries and a time-to-live of 3600 seconds. At query time the runner scores each stored exchange with a weighted combination: 0.4 times Jaccard similarity over lowercase regex word tokens of length greater than one, 0.3 times temporal decay computed as two raised to the negative age in seconds divided by 86400, 0.2 times capped logarithmic access frequency, and 0.1 times a static importance flag. The top ten ranked candidates are considered; each displayed exchange is capped at 500 characters. Packing is greedy and whole-item: the runner appends a formatted exchange only if it fits entirely within the remaining section budget alongside the section header; otherwise it skips that item and continues to the next candidate. This whole-item policy avoids presenting partial facts but may leave unused budget if the next item is too large. The architecture defines L2 and L3 classes, but this Rail does not route writes to them, does not persist entries across process restarts, and does not synchronise a team. MemGPT's tiered virtual-context management is cited as conceptual context for the storage vocabulary [[cite:ref_959d6858d034c6e1]], but the present implementation does not replicate its autonomous controller.

Each public-data question receives its own fact episode and fresh agent instances. For the baseline, facts are written directly to disk. For the enhanced arm, the runner conducts model-backed memory-writing conversations: each fact episode is presented as a user turn, the model produces an assistant acknowledgement, and the completed exchange is stored in L1. This seeding phase requires [[metric:public_small.enhanced.seed_model_calls]] model calls per budget and is the source of the write-cost asymmetry. The formal question then uses a new conversation ID so that no seeding dialogue leaks into the query context. The runner verifies isolated query history and confirms actual memory injection before scoring. Arm execution order is alternated across questions to control for potential API-level rate-limiting or temporal drift during the run; because agents are instantiated fresh per question, there is no cross-question shared state contamination to mitigate. Both query-time token usage and memory-write token usage are recorded separately. Latency measurements include the write phase and are amortised over the paired observations. Correctness is assessed by accepted-answer string matching against a predefined answer list; evidence recall requires the complete target fact to survive prompt truncation and appear in the injected context. The evaluation design adapts the single-session extraction paradigm of LongMemEval [[cite:ref_ab2c226739f2f52a]], though the resulting slice is not the official benchmark.

The evaluation uses an adapted LongMemEval-S single-session-user slice. Twenty unique questions are converted into fixed fact episodes, each containing a target answer turn and distractor turns. The same twenty questions are evaluated at two character budgets. The model is qwen-plus throughout. Metrics are answer accuracy (accepted-answer string match), complete evidence recall (target fact present in injected context), total tokens including memory writes, query-only tokens, query latency, and end-to-end latency including writes. Scoring uses deterministic string matching; no semantic judge is applied. One run is executed per budget per arm. The renderer inserts a protocol table and a cost decomposition figure; the prose below refers to them descriptively. The L1 store capacity is limited to twenty entries. If a fact episode contained more than twenty exchanges, earlier facts could be evicted before the query phase, confounding retrieval quality with first-in-first-out eviction. In this experiment the maximum number of facts per episode did not exceed the L1 capacity during seeding, so no eviction occurred. However, this constraint means the findings apply only to workloads where the fact count per session remains within the store limit.

The restricted-budget condition allocates [[metric:public_small.context_chars]] characters to the full memory section. There are [[metric:public_small.unique_questions]] unique questions, [[metric:public_small.repeats]] repeat per question, yielding [[metric:public_small.paired_observations]] paired observations. At this budget the baseline's prefix-truncation policy structurally disadvantages it, as defined in the method section: the metadata consumes a fixed portion of the allowance, and the deterministic prefix order means that later facts in the serialised file are systematically excluded. The enhanced arm's whole-item packing can select relevant items from any position in the store, provided each fits within the remaining budget. Metrics recorded include answer accuracy, complete evidence recall, total tokens (query plus seed writes), tokens per question, query latency in milliseconds, and end-to-end latency including the write phase. The small budget is the condition under which the prefix-truncation confound is most acute, and results at this budget should be interpreted with that structural asymmetry in mind.

The expanded-budget condition allocates [[metric:public_large.context_chars]] characters to the full memory section, using the same [[metric:public_large.unique_questions]] questions with [[metric:public_large.repeats]] repeat, producing [[metric:public_large.paired_observations]] paired observations. At this budget the baseline can accommodate more of the serialised file, reducing the fraction of facts lost to truncation. However, prefix order still determines which facts survive: facts appearing early in the file are always retained, while those near the end remain vulnerable if the file exceeds the budget. The enhanced arm's packing behaviour is unchanged in logic but benefits from the larger budget by fitting more whole items. The same metrics are recorded: answer accuracy, complete evidence recall, total tokens including writes, tokens per question, query latency, and end-to-end latency. The expanded budget tests whether the accuracy gap observed at the restricted budget persists when the baseline is no longer structurally starved of context space.

This section reports paired outcomes for both budget conditions. All figures derive from a single run per arm per budget. Wilson intervals describe binomial uncertainty over the twenty selected questions; they do not estimate variability across repeated model runs. The renderer inserts a question-level heatmap and full question-ID audit; the prose below summarises the aggregate patterns and notable individual cases.

The enhanced rail achieves accuracy of [[metric:public_small.enhanced.accuracy]] and evidence recall of [[metric:public_small.enhanced.evidence_recall]], with [[metric:public_small.enhanced.correct]] correct out of [[metric:public_small.enhanced.n]]. The accuracy gain is [[metric:public_small.accuracy_gain_pp]] percentage points. The paired decomposition shows [[metric:public_small.paired.both_correct]] both-correct, [[metric:public_small.paired.enhanced_only]] enhanced-only, [[metric:public_small.paired.baseline_only]] baseline-only, and [[metric:public_small.paired.both_wrong]] both-wrong outcomes. The baseline's zero accuracy is consistent with deterministic prefix truncation removing every target fact from the prompt at this budget; all twenty baseline answers are the string UNKNOWN. The enhanced arm's [[metric:public_small.paired.both_wrong]] failures correspond to questions where the target fact was not retrieved into the top-ten candidates or did not fit the remaining budget, yielding zero evidence recall in those cases. No enhanced answer was correct without full evidence ([[metric:public_small.enhanced.correct_without_full_evidence]] cases) and no enhanced answer was wrong despite full evidence ([[metric:public_small.enhanced.wrong_with_full_evidence]] cases), indicating tight coupling between evidence presence and answer correctness in this arm.

These intervals reflect question-sampling uncertainty over twenty items, not repeated-run variability. The accuracy gain narrows to [[metric:public_large.accuracy_gain_pp]] percentage points. The baseline recovers from zero to twelve correct answers because the larger budget admits more of the serialised file, yet seven questions remain beyond the prefix boundary. The single both-wrong case concerns a dog-breed question where neither arm retrieved the target fact. Notably, the baseline records [[metric:public_large.baseline.correct_without_full_evidence]] correct answer without complete evidence recall: a partial fact fragment still contained the accepted answer string, demonstrating that strict evidence recall is not a necessary condition for correctness under string-match scoring. The enhanced arm shows zero correct-without-full-evidence and zero wrong-with-full-evidence cases.

Cost-per-correct-answer provides additional context for the trade-off. At the restricted budget, the baseline's cost per correct answer is undefined due to division by zero correct responses, while the enhanced arm expends approximately 7820 tokens per correct answer (total tokens [[metric:public_small.enhanced.all_tokens]] divided by [[metric:public_small.enhanced.correct]]). At the expanded budget, the baseline spends roughly 1406 tokens per correct answer (total tokens [[metric:public_large.baseline.all_tokens]] divided by [[metric:public_large.baseline.correct]]), whereas the enhanced arm spends approximately 13896 tokens per correct answer (total tokens [[metric:public_large.enhanced.all_tokens]] divided by [[metric:public_large.enhanced.correct]]). This yields a cost-per-correct-answer ratio of approximately 9.9 at the expanded budget. The total token cost per question for the enhanced arm is approximately 15.6 to 21.7 times higher than the baseline's, computed directly from the tokens-per-question values: [[metric:public_small.enhanced.tokens_per_question]] divided by [[metric:public_small.baseline.tokens_per_question]] at the restricted budget, and [[metric:public_large.enhanced.tokens_per_question]] divided by [[metric:public_large.baseline.tokens_per_question]] at the expanded budget. These ratios confirm that the accuracy advantage carries a substantial absolute token expenditure that must be weighed against deployment constraints.

The results support a clear engineering interpretation: selective retrieval from working memory buys accuracy over prefix-truncated file access, but the purchase price is paid in model-backed memory-construction calls. At the restricted budget the baseline is structurally unable to present any target fact, so the observed [[metric:public_small.accuracy_gain_pp]]-percentage-point gap reflects information absence rather than a difference in retrieval ranking quality. At the expanded budget the baseline recovers most facts, yet the residual [[metric:public_large.accuracy_gain_pp]]-percentage-point gap persists because whole-item packing can surface facts from any serialisation position while the prefix remains order-bound. This distinction matters for practitioners: the gap is not solely a retrieval-quality effect but partly a format and packing effect.

Item-level analysis of the seven enhanced-only cases at the expanded budget clarifies the mechanism behind the residual gap. Diagnostic traces show that for questions such as vintage camera collecting duration, Japan trip length, meeting location for Sophia, community theater play attendance, sister's birthday gift, shampoo brand, and music streaming service, the baseline returned UNKNOWN while the enhanced arm produced the correct answer. In each of these cases, the target fact was positioned late enough in the serialised JIUWENSWARM.md file that it fell beyond the [[metric:public_large.context_chars]]-character prefix boundary. The enhanced arm's Jaccard-weighted ranking successfully elevated these late-positioned facts into the top-ten candidates, and the expanded budget provided sufficient room for the whole-item packer to include them. This pattern confirms that the residual gap is driven by serialisation order rather than a fundamental inability of the baseline model to reason about the facts when they are present. Conversely, the single both-wrong case at the expanded budget involves a dog-breed question where the target fact was apparently not retrieved by the enhanced arm's lexical scorer and also fell outside the baseline's prefix window, suggesting that low lexical overlap between the query and the stored exchange can defeat the Jaccard component regardless of budget size.

The seven both-wrong cases at the restricted budget and the single both-wrong case at the expanded budget for the enhanced arm indicate retrieval failures independent of budget size. Examining diagnostic cases such as the community theater play and the dog breed reveals that these failures likely stem from insufficient lexical overlap between the query phrasing and the stored exchange text, causing the Jaccard similarity component to assign low scores. Additionally, the 500-character item cap may have truncated relevant context in some exchanges, although the primary failure mode appears to be ranking rather than packing exclusion. Without an offline ablation varying the Jaccard weight, temporal decay rate, or frequency cap, the precise contribution of each ranking component cannot be isolated. The distractor density in the fact episodes may also dilute lexical signals, but this hypothesis requires controlled variation of distractor counts that was not performed.

Several confounds limit attribution. First, the smaller budget disadvantages the baseline through file-metadata overhead and deterministic prefix loss; this is a structural confound, not a neutral design choice. Second, the two arms differ in presentation format—flat file with metadata versus formatted user-assistant exchanges—and the model may respond differently to dialogue format independent of information content. Third, no offline retrieval ablation was performed: the Jaccard weight, temporal-decay rate, and frequency cap were not varied, so the contribution of individual ranking components is unknown. Budget sensitivity is tested; component sensitivity is not. Fourth, string-match scoring may miss paraphrastic correct answers; semantic review of the both-wrong cases has not been conducted.

The evidence-recall pattern informs RQ2. In the enhanced arm, accuracy and complete evidence recall are numerically identical at both budgets, and zero cases of correct-without-full-evidence or wrong-with-full-evidence are observed. In the baseline at the expanded budget, one question is answered correctly despite incomplete evidence recall, showing that a partial fact fragment can contain the accepted answer string. This asymmetry suggests that whole-item packing enforces a tighter coupling between evidence presence and answer generation, whereas prefix truncation can produce partial fragments that coincidentally match the answer. The cost-per-correct-answer metric further contextualises RQ3: while the enhanced arm achieves higher raw accuracy, it spends approximately 9.9 times more tokens per correct answer at the expanded budget compared to the baseline. Whether this expenditure is justified depends on the application's tolerance for incorrect answers versus its token budget constraints. A system that writes once and queries hundreds of times amortises the construction cost effectively, whereas a system that rebuilds memory each session pays the full price repeatedly.

The study's limitations are structural rather than incidental. One run per budget precludes any estimate of model stochasticity or sensitivity to fact-episode ordering. The twenty-question slice is drawn from a single-session extraction adaptation and does not cover multi-session reasoning, temporal updates, or abstention. L2 and L3 persistence, cross-restart durability, and team synchronisation are architectural stubs not exercised here. The adapted LongMemEval slice is not an official benchmark score. No claim is made about the automatic paper writer or any end-to-end generation pipeline. These boundaries define the scope within which the findings are actionable.

Returning to the three research questions: RQ1, under equal full-section character budgets, the hybrid lexical-selection rail achieves higher answer accuracy than the prefix-truncated file baseline by [[metric:public_small.accuracy_gain_pp]] percentage points at the restricted budget and [[metric:public_large.accuracy_gain_pp]] percentage points at the expanded budget. Item-level diagnostics confirm that the residual gap at the expanded budget corresponds to facts positioned late in the baseline's serialised file, which the enhanced arm's ranking successfully retrieves. RQ2, complete evidence recall is a near-necessary condition for correctness in the enhanced arm at both budgets; the baseline can occasionally answer correctly from a partial fact fragment at the expanded budget, but this is the exception rather than the rule. RQ3, the enhanced arm's total token cost per question is approximately 15.6 to 21.7 times higher than the baseline's, computed from the supplied tokens-per-question values, and the cost per correct answer is approximately 9.9 times higher at the expanded budget. These ratios are driven entirely by the [[metric:public_small.enhanced.seed_model_calls]] model-backed memory-write calls; query-time tokens alone do not explain the cost gap.

Retrieved memory buys accuracy, but the purchase price is write-time model cost. The trade-off narrows as the character budget grows because the file baseline recovers facts that were previously truncated, yet it does not vanish within the tested range because whole-item packing avoids the partial-fact failures that prefix truncation produces. These are single-run descriptive findings on an adapted twenty-question slice evaluated with string-match scoring. Future work requires repeated runs to estimate model stochasticity, offline component ablations to isolate ranking contributions, format-controlled comparisons to separate presentation effects from information effects, and evaluation on the full official LongMemEval benchmark covering multi-session reasoning, temporal updates, and abstention.
